text:
# The Spark
Quick, bright, and always starting something.
Cheerful by disposition. Restless by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Speaks up, Open-handed, Light-hearted

## Your type
You bring energy. Your mood is light and you hate sitting still. You would rather try something and laugh about it later than wait and wonder. People catch your enthusiasm. A quiet week makes you restless, and a full one makes you happy.
Where the trap is set for you: pleasure. "For because pleasure borders on mirth, he holds out lust as a bait to cheerful dispositions." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like a good time. One more drink, one more episode, one more look than you meant to give.
What you bring: You get things going. You make hard things feel lighter. You bounce back fast.
What it costs you: You start more than you finish. You can rush past what needed thought. Quiet feels like a threat, so you fill it.
Kindred: Augustine, as a young man: Before his conversion he loved talk, jokes, reading together and friendly arguments. He was just as honest, later, about where his love of pleasure had led him.
Your opposite: The Deep Well (Thoughtful, grave, and feels things all the way down.)

## Your leanings
- Mood: Light-hearted <-> Heavy-hearted: Light-hearted (17/100)
- Nerve: Confident <-> Careful: balanced (54/100)
- Make-up: Restless mind <-> Quiet mind: Restless mind (4/100)
- Talk: Speaks up <-> Keeps it in: Speaks up (0/100)
- Candour: Says it plainly <-> Chooses what to show: Says it plainly (33/100)
- When wronged: Lets them know <-> Lets it go: Lets it go (83/100)
- Temper: Fiery <-> Gentle: Gentle (75/100)
- Disagreements: Takes a stand <-> Keeps the peace: Keeps the peace (83/100)
- Pace: Rushes in <-> Puts it off: Rushes in (33/100)
- Follow-through: Hard to start <-> Hard to finish: Hard to start (33/100)
- Little things: Careful with little things <-> Easy on little things: balanced (42/100)
- Your own work: Sure of your work <-> Hard on yourself: balanced (50/100)
- Correction: Say it straight <-> A hint is enough: A hint is enough (75/100)
- Room: Takes up room <-> Makes yourself small: Takes up room (33/100)
- Your mind: Holds firm <-> Easily swayed: Holds firm (33/100)
- Others' wins: Simply glad <-> Feels the sting: Simply glad (17/100)
- Seen and unseen: Better in public <-> Better in private: balanced (42/100)
- After a mistake: Dwells on a mistake <-> Moves on: balanced (42/100)
- Having: Open-handed <-> Careful with what you have: Open-handed (8/100)
- Comforts: Enjoys comforts <-> Keeps a tight rein: Enjoys comforts (25/100)
Most like you: Speaks up, Open-handed, Light-hearted. Balanced: Your own work, After a mistake, Seen and unseen
* Speaks up: You think out loud, and you are easy to talk to. What you may not see: Much talk scatters the mind, Gregory says, so it loses touch with itself. And idle talk slides, step by step, into talk about other people. "it has no power to turn back within to the knowledge of itself" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Before you speak, ask whether it is needed, or kind.
* Open-handed: You give easily. What you may not see: Gregory warns the generous against giving so much at once that they run short and start grumbling. "when the soul of the giver knows not how to endure want, then, in withdrawing much from himself, he seeks out against himself occasion of impatience" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Give steadily and cheerfully, and do not keep score.
* Light-hearted: Your mood is light. Things rarely get you down for long. What you may not see: Gregory says pleasure sits right next door to cheerfulness. The pull you are least guarded against is the pull of a good time.  Counsel: Enjoy what you are given. Keep an eye on what lives next door.

## What you might not have noticed
- You said you let rudeness go. You also said hours later you think of what you should have said. You win in the moment by staying calm. Then, on a quiet evening, it comes back bigger than it was. You can end up wishing you had been harsher than you would ever actually be. The hard part for you is not staying calm. It is the evening after. "blushes for having borne such things calmly, and is sorry that he did not return insults" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you let things slide that you probably should not. You also said you calm things down when friends argue. Gregory says gentleness has a next-door neighbour, and it is letting things go that should not go. Keeping the peace can be love. It can also be the easier road. "Sloth is frequently looked upon as a maintenance of peace" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said you are nothing but glad when friends succeed. You also said you admire lots of people you never try to be like. That gladness is rare and good. Gregory’s one warning is for people exactly like you: do not only cheer from the stands. Admire it enough to try it. "eager backers, but inert spectators" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said your mood is usually light. You also said after a hard day you treat yourself. A light heart is a gift. Gregory adds one warning: pleasure lives right next door to cheerfulness, so it is the one pull you are least guarded against. "For because pleasure borders on mirth, he holds out lust as a bait to cheerful dispositions." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)

## How your anger works
Slow and brief. It takes a lot to anger you, and it does not last. Gregory says this is the one closest to peace of mind.  One caution from Chrysostom: calm that is never tested is not yet patience. Stay among people.

## How you speak
Fluent, not deep. Words come easily, sometimes before the thought is ready. Of the four kinds of speaker, Gregory blames only this one, and says it needs holding back. The fix is simple: think first.

## How to help me
1. Ask for my help. I will give it gladly.
2. Give me room to think out loud.
3. Show me. Let me see someone do it.
4. Slow me down. I run ahead.
5. Tell me what I did well. It makes me try harder.
6. Pick the one thing that matters most, and let the rest go.
7. Tell me in private.

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
Right now: Gluttony. Not eating well. Reaching for food or drink to take the edge off, or wanting something nicer than what is in front of you. Gregory says the fault is never in the food. It is in the wanting. How it talks to you: "God has created all things clean, in order to be eaten" (Gregory, Moralia on Job, gluttony’s own speech) How it shows: Eating when you are not hungry. Wanting the dish to be different. A heavy, dull mind afterwards. What feeds it: It comes first on Cassian’s list, and it opens the door to the others. What takes its place: Cassian’s advice is steady, daily moderation, not sudden strict fasts. And break your own fast gladly for a guest.
All eight: Gluttony 100, Vainglory 66, Pride 63, Listlessness 56, Sadness 45, Greed 36, Lust 12, Anger 12. Troubles you least: Anger.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Diligence: You keep working when others stop. Counterfeit: Restlessness. Not being able to stop can feel like faithfulness. "Restlessness of spirit is frequently termed a watchful solicitude" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your strength: Courage. Its partner: Counsel. You act bravely. The risk is acting before you have thought it through.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your gladness is a gift. Kept close to God, it becomes the joy Christ promised, the kind nobody can take from you. "I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man shall take from you" (Christ, quoted by Gregory in the Pastoral Rule)
Your line: The Host (hospitality). You serve by opening your door. A meal, a bed, a welcome. People feel at home with you. Cassian names Abraham and Lot, and in his own day Macarius, who ran a guest house in Alexandria and was known as "a man of singular courtesy and patience". Second: The Watcher.
(They picked: gladly do: Have them over and cook them a meal. / Pray for them every day, without telling them.; people come for: Money, or something they need. / A place to stay, or a meal.)

# The Still Water
Listens first, keeps the peace, and thinks it through.
Careful by disposition. Quiet by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Hard to start, Careful with what you have, Keeps it in

## Your type
You take things in before you let anything out. You would rather listen than talk, and you would rather keep the peace than win. A crowded week wears you down faster than it does most people. Give you quiet and you do your best thinking. People trust you, because you are careful with them.
Where the trap is set for you: fear. "Because the timid dread punishments, he threatens terrors to the fearful." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like worry. What if they are upset? What if it goes wrong? What if I say it, and it costs me?
What you bring: You listen, and people can tell. You are slow to judge out loud. You rarely make an enemy.
What it costs you: You say less than you mean. You carry hurts home with you. You wait to be sure, and sometimes the moment passes.
Kindred: St Gregory the Theologian: He loved "calm and retirement" from his youth, and ran away when they made him a priest. When his best friend Basil called him lazy, he wrote back: "My greatest business always is to keep free from business." Near the end he said, "I am weary of being charged with my gentleness." | Jeremiah: When God called him, he pleaded that he was too young to speak. Gregory says he held back out of love: he longed to stay close to God in quiet. | Abba Arsenius: A desert monk who fled the world to pray. In an old story he is seen sailing in silence, with the Spirit of God beside him.
Your opposite: The Herald (Steps forward, speaks up, and gets things moving.)

* Hard to start: The first step is the hardest part. What you may not see: Gregory says people who never begin are usually busy with something else they love. That has to be seen for what it is first.  Counsel: Name what is holding you back. Then take one step.
* Careful with what you have: You keep a little back. What you may not see: Holding on can call itself thrift. Gregory adds that grasping often grows from fear of running short. "Tenacity is sometimes considered frugality" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Give something away this week that you might have kept.
* Keeps it in: You listen more than you talk. What you may not see: The talking does not stop. It moves inside, where nobody can answer it. "more grievous loquacity in the heart" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Your mouth needs a door, not a wall: something that opens as well as shuts.

## What you might not have noticed
- You said your gut says “let me think” when a friend asks for money. You also said you keep a little money back, just in case. Gregory says grasping grows from two roots, pride and fear, and yours looks like fear. It is not greed for more. It is fear of less. That is worth knowing, because fear is answered differently from greed. "avarice sometimes steals upon men from pride, and sometimes from apprehension" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said you listen more than you talk. You also said you have whole conversations in your head that never happen. Those are the same thing. The talking does not stop. It moves inside, where nobody can answer back. And an argument nobody can answer is easy to win. It can leave you quietly judging people who never got to reply. "For his tongue he represses, his mind he exalts" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you let rudeness go. You also said hours later you think of what you should have said. You win in the moment by staying calm. Then, on a quiet evening, it comes back bigger than it was. You can end up wishing you had been harsher than you would ever actually be. The hard part for you is not staying calm. It is the evening after. "blushes for having borne such things calmly, and is sorry that he did not return insults" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you hold back after a hard day. You also said you notice when other people overindulge. Gregory says self-denial has its own temptation, and it is not food. It is looking down on people who do not go without. Discipline is a gift. Judging the undisciplined is where it turns. "the pride of abstinence" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)

## How your anger works
Hard wood. It takes a lot to make you angry. But once it is lit, it stays lit. It just burns where no one can see it. "others, like the heavier and harder kinds of wood, are slow in taking fire, but being once kindled, are with difficulty put out" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Gregory’s cure for your kind is to see it coming. Before the day starts, think through what might go wrong and how you will meet it calmly. A blow you expected lands softer.

## How you speak
Deep, but held in. You think deeply, but the words come hard. Gregory knew this speaker and did not blame them. He said they need help getting it out. Try writing it down first, or saying it to one person instead of a room.

## How to help me
1. Explain why. I need the reasons.
2. Give me a push. I am slow to get going.
3. Ask what I think. I rarely offer it.
4. Say "next time, try this", not "you did this wrong".
5. Point out everything. I would rather know.
6. Argue it out with me. Win fairly and I will come round.
7. Tell me plainly what you need.

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
Right now: Greed. Not always wanting more. Often it is fear of having less. Cassian says it starts with "excellent and almost reasonable excuses". How it talks to you: "It is a very blameless thing, that thou desirest some things to possess; because thou seekest not to be increased, but art afraid of being in want" (Gregory, Moralia on Job, greed’s own speech) How it shows: Keeping a reserve "just in case". Worrying about old age and illness. It is never quite enough. What feeds it: Gregory says sadness runs down into it: a heart with no joy inside looks for comfort in owning things. What takes its place: Cassian says cut the desire, not only the spending. Be content with what you need.
All eight: Greed 100, Sadness 83, Listlessness 72, Pride 63, Gluttony 46, Anger 41, Vainglory 18, Lust 12. Troubles you least: Lust.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Thrift: You take care of what you have been given. Counterfeit: Holding on. Tightness can call itself good sense. "niggardliness palliates itself under the name of frugality" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your care is a gift. Gregory says the fearful should not stay in fear but grow, fed by love, until love does what fear used to do. "grow up by the nursing of charity to the grace of love" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
Your line: The Teacher (teaching). You serve by helping people understand. You explain, you make it clear, you pass it on. Cassian names people who "give themselves up to teaching" as one of the lines God gives. Second: The Giver.
(They picked: gladly do: Quietly pay for something they can’t afford. / Explain something until they finally understand it.; people come for: Someone to take charge and sort things out. / Something explained or taught.)

# The Hearth
Warm, steady, and glad to be where you are.
Cheerful by disposition. Quiet by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Keeps the peace, Hard to finish, Sure of your work

## Your type
You are easy to be around. Your mood is light, and you do not need to be busy to be happy. People relax when you walk in. You enjoy things as they come: a meal, a long talk, an evening at home. You do not go looking for trouble, and it rarely finds you.
Where the trap is set for you: pleasure. "For because pleasure borders on mirth, he holds out lust as a bait to cheerful dispositions." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like a good time. One more drink, one more episode, one more look than you meant to give.
What you bring: People feel welcome around you. You enjoy the good things you are given. You do not make things harder than they are.
What it costs you: You can settle for comfortable. You would rather not look at what is wrong. Pleasure can quietly become the point.
Kindred: St Antony the Great: He spent twenty years alone in the desert. When he came out, Athanasius says, his friends were amazed at how settled he was, and his face was cheerful because his soul was at peace.
Your opposite: The Forge (Intense, driven, and cannot stand things done badly.)

- Nerve: Confident <-> Careful: Careful (63/100)

* Keeps the peace: You calm things down. What you may not see: Gregory warns the peaceable not to love peace so much that they never tell anyone they are wrong. "Break outward peace with him, but guard in your heart’s core internal peace concerning him" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: You can disagree with someone and still keep the peace inside you.
* Hard to finish: You start well, then fade. What you may not see: Gregory says a soul is like a boat going upstream. Stop rowing and it does not stay put. It drifts back. "in the condition of a ship ascending against the stream of a river" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Finish one thing before you start the next.
* Sure of your work: You know when you have done well. What you may not see: The confident, Gregory says, count everything they do as excellent, and bristle when corrected. "Those count all they do to be singularly eminent" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Ask someone you trust what could be better.

- You said you let things slide that you probably should not. You also said you calm things down when friends argue. Gregory says gentleness has a next-door neighbour, and it is letting things go that should not go. Keeping the peace can be love. It can also be the easier road. "Sloth is frequently looked upon as a maintenance of peace" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said your mood is usually light. You also said after a hard day you treat yourself. A light heart is a gift. Gregory adds one warning: pleasure lives right next door to cheerfulness, so it is the one pull you are least guarded against. "For because pleasure borders on mirth, he holds out lust as a bait to cheerful dispositions." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said you are nothing but glad when friends succeed. You also said you admire lots of people you never try to be like. That gladness is rare and good. - You said more of your regrets are things you never got round to. You also said before something big you think about what could go wrong. Those are one habit. You picture the setbacks, and the picture keeps you still. Gregory quotes Proverbs about a farmer who would not plough because it was cold, and then had nothing to harvest. "The sluggard would not plough by reason of the cold" (Proverbs, as Gregory quotes it)

Kindled reeds. Your anger flares and is gone. You rarely hold a grudge. The danger is the first minute: what you say before it burns out. 2. Explain why. I need the reasons.
3. Give me a push. I am slow to get going.
4. Tell me what I did well. It makes me try harder.
5. Point out everything. I would rather know.
6. Tell me in private.
7. Argue it out with me. Win fairly and I will come round.

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
Right now: Greed. Not always wanting more. Often it is fear of having less. Cassian says it starts with "excellent and almost reasonable excuses". How it talks to you: "It is a very blameless thing, that thou desirest some things to possess; because thou seekest not to be increased, but art afraid of being in want" (Gregory, Moralia on Job, greed’s own speech) How it shows: Keeping a reserve "just in case". Worrying about old age and illness. It is never quite enough. What feeds it: Gregory says sadness runs down into it: a heart with no joy inside looks for comfort in owning things. What takes its place: Cassian says cut the desire, not only the spending. Be content with what you need.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Peace: You calm things. People are safer around you. Counterfeit: Avoidance. Staying out of trouble can pass for keeping the peace. "Sloth is frequently looked upon as a maintenance of peace" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your gladness is a gift. Kept close to God, it becomes the joy Christ promised, the kind nobody can take from you. "I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man shall take from you" (Christ, quoted by Gregory in the Pastoral Rule)
Your line: The Host (hospitality). You serve by opening your door. A meal, a bed, a welcome. People feel at home with you. Cassian names Abraham and Lot, and in his own day Macarius, who ran a guest house in Alexandria and was known as "a man of singular courtesy and patience". Second: The Caregiver.

Serious by disposition. Quiet by make-up.

"For his tongue he represses, his mind he exalts" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)

"nor is a debtor absolved by not increasing his debt, unless he also pays what he has incurred" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)

Deep, but held in. You think deeply, but the words come hard. Gregory knew this speaker and did not blame them. He said they need help getting it out. Try writing it down first, or saying it to one person instead of a room.

1. Explain why. I need the reasons.

6. Ask for my help. I will give it gladly.
7. Say "next time, try this", not "you did this wrong".

How it talks to you: "The things that are done to thee cannot be borne patiently; nay rather, patiently to endure them is a sin" (Gregory, Moralia on Job, anger’s own speech) How it shows: Replaying what someone did. Going cold on people while saying you are fine. Irritation at things that cannot help it. What feeds it: Cassian says greed feeds it. Gregory says envy does. What takes its place: Cassian says its place is taken by patience.
Close behind: Sadness.

Thrift: You take care of what you have been given. Counterfeit: Holding on. Tightness can call itself good sense. "niggardliness palliates itself under the name of frugality" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.

Your seriousness is not a flaw to be fixed. Held under reason, the fire in it becomes holy zeal. "For some are possessed by anger, but while they submit this to reason, they convert it into service rendered to holy zeal." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your line: The Teacher (teaching). You serve by helping people understand. You explain, you make it clear, you pass it on. Cassian names people who "give themselves up to teaching" as one of the lines God gives. Second: The Caregiver.
